promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: A city in a developing/emerging country

questions.q: What is urbanisation?
options: The increase in the proportion of a population living in urban areas
The movement of people from cities to the countryside
The growth of farming in rural areas
The decline of city populations over time
questions.explain: Urbanisation is the rising share of a population living in towns and cities.

questions.q: A megacity is usually defined as a city with a population of at least:
options: 1 million
5 million
10 million
50 million
questions.explain: Megacities are defined as urban areas with populations of 10 million or more.

questions.q: Which of the following is a push factor encouraging rural-urban migration?
options: Better paid jobs in the city
Drought and crop failure in the countryside
Higher quality healthcare in the city
Better schools in the city
questions.explain: Push factors are negative conditions in rural areas, such as drought, that force people to leave.

questions.q: The movement of people from the countryside to live in cities is called:
options: Counter-urbanisation
Suburbanisation
Rural-urban migration
Re-urbanisation
questions.explain: Rural-urban migration is the movement of people from rural areas into urban areas.

questions.q: Suburbanisation is best described as:
options: The movement of people and businesses from the inner city to the outer edges of the city
The movement of people from cities to rural villages
The rapid growth of informal settlements
The return of people to regenerated city centres
questions.explain: Suburbanisation is the outward spread of people and activity to the edges of a city.

questions.q: Counter-urbanisation refers to:
options: People moving from rural areas into cities
People moving out of cities to live in rural areas
The growth of the world's largest cities
The redevelopment of derelict inner-city land
questions.explain: Counter-urbanisation is the movement of people away from cities into rural areas.

questions.q: Why is the rate of urbanisation now generally slow in developed countries such as the UK?
options: They have very high birth rates
They are already highly urbanised, with most people already living in towns and cities
They have no cities
Rural areas are growing faster than cities everywhere
questions.explain: Developed countries urbanised long ago, so few people remain to move from rural to urban areas.

questions.q: A country's urban population rises from 30% to 55% over 40 years, mainly as young adults leave farms for factory work in cities. This best illustrates:
options: Counter-urbanisation
Rapid urbanisation driven by rural-urban migration
Suburbanisation
Deindustrialisation
questions.explain: A rising urban share fed by people leaving farms for city jobs is rapid urbanisation through rural-urban migration.

questions.q: Areas of poor-quality, often self-built housing that develop illegally on the edges of cities in emerging countries are known as:
options: Central business districts
Informal (squatter) settlements
Greenfield sites
Commuter villages
questions.explain: Informal or squatter settlements are unplanned, self-built housing areas lacking legal land rights.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the informal economy in a rapidly growing city?
options: Work that is taxed and officially recorded by the government
Jobs such as street selling that are unregulated, untaxed and often insecure
Highly paid jobs in large multinational offices
Government-run public services
questions.explain: The informal economy consists of unregulated, untaxed and often insecure work like street trading.

questions.q: Natural increase in a population is calculated as:
options: Birth rate minus death rate
Immigration minus emigration
Birth rate plus death rate
Total population divided by area
questions.explain: Natural increase is the birth rate minus the death rate over a given period.

questions.q: Which of the following is a common challenge caused by rapid urbanisation in emerging cities?
options: A shortage of people to fill jobs
Pressure on housing, services and infrastructure leading to overcrowding
Declining city populations
Too much green space
questions.explain: Rapid growth often outpaces the supply of housing and services, causing overcrowding and strain on infrastructure.

questions.q: A city government upgrades an informal settlement by providing legal land rights, clean water and paved roads instead of demolishing it. This approach is best described as:
options: Forced eviction
A site-and-service or self-help improvement scheme
Counter-urbanisation
Deindustrialisation
questions.explain: Providing services and land rights so residents can improve their own homes is a self-help / site-and-service scheme.

questions.q: Deindustrialisation in UK cities refers to:
options: The building of many new factories
The decline of manufacturing industry and loss of factory jobs
The growth of farming
The movement of people into the city centre
questions.explain: Deindustrialisation is the loss of manufacturing industry and associated factory employment.

questions.q: Gentrification of an inner-city area typically involves:
options: Wealthier people moving in and improving run-down housing, often raising property prices
The demolition of all housing to build factories
Poorer residents moving into new social housing
The closure of all local shops and services
questions.explain: Gentrification is wealthier residents renovating older housing, which tends to push up property prices.

questions.q: Urban regeneration is:
options: The natural growth of a city's population
The improvement and redevelopment of run-down urban areas
The movement of people to rural areas
The spread of a city into surrounding countryside
questions.explain: Regeneration is the renewal and redevelopment of derelict or declining urban areas.

questions.q: Re-urbanisation occurs when:
options: People and investment move back into city centres, often following regeneration
Cities spread outwards into the countryside
People leave cities permanently for rural areas
Birth rates in rural areas rise sharply
questions.explain: Re-urbanisation is the return of people and investment to city centres, frequently after regeneration.

questions.q: A former UK dockland with derelict warehouses is redeveloped into flats, offices and leisure facilities, attracting new residents and businesses. This is an example of:
options: Deindustrialisation
Urban regeneration
Rural-urban migration
Counter-urbanisation
questions.explain: Redeveloping derelict industrial land into new housing and business use is urban regeneration.

questions.q: The 'situation' of a city refers to:
options: The actual land the city is built on
Its position in relation to surrounding features such as rivers, roads and other settlements
The number of people living there
The age of its buildings
questions.explain: Situation describes a settlement's position relative to surrounding physical and human features, unlike site.

questions.q: Which measure would most help make a city more environmentally sustainable?
options: Encouraging more private car use
Investing in efficient public transport and recycling schemes
Building on all remaining green space
Increasing energy use per person
questions.explain: Public transport and recycling reduce pollution and waste, making urban living more sustainable.
